blindSummary: This state/province sits within the twelve-jurisdiction bloc whose religious criminal-law system was adopted between 1999 and 2002. Religious courts hold criminal jurisdiction over adherents of the locally dominant faith, and the religious penal code extends criminalisation to same-sex acts between women, which the federal statute does not cover independently. No trans-specific incident or morality-police documentation exists for this state/province in the record. The legal architecture is the finding; under-reporting is structural (a national monitoring group and a foreign government's information note both flag data limitations). The enacted parallel criminal system - capital-capable on the statute book - is what a visitor of the locally dominant faith, or one perceived to adhere to it, would face.
blindSourceSummaries: An international human-rights organisation's report (2004) on the extension of religious criminal law: the first jurisdiction in the bloc enacted its religious-law establishment statute on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve jurisdictions had adopted some form of religious criminal law into their legislation - to date the only ones where religious courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

blindTangential: Same-sex conduct criminalisation is the adjacent layer here: a 2014 federal statute (up to 14 years, applies to visitors) plus the parallel religious-law penal layer for adherents of the locally dominant faith shape police and morality-police posture toward any gender-nonconforming presence, even though the written offences target conduct rather than gender identity.
